hypotheses.text: Prenatal head circumference and neurosonography cannot definitively differentiate PLAA-related neurodevelopmental disorder from pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH), as classic PCH subtypes frequently exhibit normal early-to-mid fetal biometric measurements with microcephaly only emerging late in gestation or postnatally.
hypotheses.rationale: A key tenet for distinguishing PLAA-associated disorder from PCH was the assumption that PCH exhibits congenital microcephaly on prenatal imaging whereas PLAA disorder shows strictly normal prenatal growth. If classic PCH also commonly presents with normal early prenatal biometry and postnatal microcephaly, normal prenatal imaging cannot serve as an exclusionary discriminator.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 42 fetuses with confirmed pontocerebellar hypoplasia, microcephaly was detected prenatally in only 4 fetuses, indicating that microcephaly is infrequently present during prenatal ultrasound screening and typically manifests at the very end of pregnancy or after birth.

evidence.text: Official clinical guidelines for pontocerebellar hypoplasia document that microcephaly is usually not apparent at birth but becomes noticeable as brain growth slows down during infancy and early childhood.

hypotheses.text: The structural distinction between PLAA deficiency and true pontocerebellar hypoplasia relies on serial morphometry demonstrating disproportionate supratentorial cerebral atrophy and delayed myelination with secondary cerebellar vermian volume loss, rather than primary pontine flattening or the classic dragonfly cerebellar hemispheric hypoplasia seen in PCH.
hypotheses.rationale: While both conditions can demonstrate progressive microcephaly and cerebellar volume loss, distinguishing them requires identifying whether the primary pathology is pontocerebellar hypoplasia (reduced transverse cerebellar diameter with flat ventral pons) or a progressive leukoencephalopathy with secondary supratentorial atrophy and vermis involution.

evidence.text: Differential diagnosis of cerebellar hypoplasia relies on categorizing cerebellar involvement (isolated vermis vs both vermis and hemispheres) and distinguishing primary brainstem/pontine hypoplasia from progressive supratentorial volume loss and cortical migration anomalies.

source.title: Diagnostic approach to cerebellar hypoplasia
source.quote: Traditionally, neuroimaging has been a key tool to categorize CH based on the pattern of cerebellar involvement (e.g., hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis only vs. hypoplasia of both the vermis and cerebellar hemispheres) and the presence of associated brainstem and cerebral anomalies.

evidence.text: Classic PCH on prenatal MRI is characterized specifically by pontine atrophy and measurements of transverse cerebellar biometry decreasing with advancing gestational age, distinguishing true pontine-involving hypoplasias from other brain malformations.

hypotheses.text: Biallelic complete loss-of-function variants in PLAA can manifest with prenatal structural cerebellar and cerebral anomalies detectable before birth, showing that normal prenatal neuroimaging is not an obligatory inclusion criterion for PLAA-related disorders across the entire mutational spectrum.
hypotheses.rationale: The conflict between earlier reports claiming completely normal birth parameters and newer prenatal exome sequencing panels that identify PLAA in fetuses with CNS malformations suggests a variant-dependent spectrum where nullizygous alleles disrupt neurogenesis early in gestation.

evidence.text: PLAA is curated within the Genomics England PanelApp panel for severe microcephaly and pontocerebellar hypoplasia alongside established fetal-onset developmental genes.

new_directions.question_text: What proportion of confirmed fetuses with biallelic PLAA pathogenic variants exhibit transverse cerebellar diameter (TCD) below the 5th percentile on second- or third-trimester fetal ultrasound?
new_directions.rationale: Directly measuring fetal biometrics across all reported prenatal PLAA cases will resolve whether cerebellar hypoplasia can be congenital in PLAA deficiency or whether it is strictly postnatal.

new_directions.question_text: Do patients with PLAA deficiency ever exhibit true pontine hypoplasia (measured by pons-to-vermis or pons-to-midbrain ratio) on brain MRI, or is the brainstem strictly preserved relative to supratentorial atrophy?
new_directions.rationale: Quantifying pontine biometry will determine if PLAA should be classified as a true pontocerebellar disorder or whether cerebellar changes represent secondary vermian atrophy.
